title: Speech Sounds & the IPA
description: How humans produce the building blocks of language

concepts.title: Vowels and Consonants
concepts.contentHtml:
Speech sounds split into two main families:

Vowels are produced with an open vocal tract — air flows freely. Their identity comes from tongue position and lip shape. 'ee' (high front), 'ah' (low back), 'oo' (high back rounded).

Consonants involve some restriction or closure — the tongue, lips, or teeth obstruct the airstream. Stop the air completely and you get a stop (p, t, k); narrow it to make turbulence and you get a fricative (f, s, sh).

Most languages have more consonants than vowels, but the ratio varies wildly.

concepts.title: The IPA — One Symbol per Sound
concepts.contentHtml:
English spelling is famously chaotic — the letters 'ough' can be pronounced six different ways (through, though, tough, cough, bough, thought).

The International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) solves this by giving every distinct human speech sound its own symbol. /θ/ is the 'th' in 'think'. /ʃ/ is the 'sh' in 'ship'. /ŋ/ is the 'ng' in 'sing'.

IPA transcriptions are written in square brackets [ ] for actual sounds, or slashes / / for phonemes (sound categories). Linguists, dictionaries, and language teachers all rely on it.

concepts.title: Place and Voicing
concepts.contentHtml:
Consonants are described by where in the mouth they're made (place of articulation):

— Bilabial — both lips (p, b, m)
— Alveolar — tongue at the ridge behind upper teeth (t, d, n, s)
— Velar — tongue at the soft palate (k, g)

And whether the vocal cords vibrate — voicing:

— Voiceless: p, t, k, s, f
— Voiced: b, d, g, z, v

Try it: feel your throat while saying 'ssss' (no vibration) then 'zzzz' (vibration). Same place, different voicing.

title: Phonological Patterns
description: Sounds in your head vs sounds in the world

concepts.title: Phonemes vs Allophones
concepts.contentHtml:
A phoneme is a sound category that distinguishes words in a language. /p/ and /b/ are different phonemes in English — 'pat' and 'bat' mean different things.

An allophone is a physical variant of a phoneme that doesn't change meaning.

Example: in 'pin' the /p/ is aspirated (puff of air — [pʰ]); in 'spin' it isn't ([p]). Hold your hand to your mouth and feel. English speakers don't notice this difference because both are the same phoneme /p/. In Hindi, [pʰ] and [p] are different phonemes — and confusing them changes the word.

concepts.title: Minimal Pairs
concepts.contentHtml:
How do you tell if two sounds are different phonemes in a language? Find a minimal pair: two words that differ in only one sound and have different meanings.

'pat' vs 'bat' — only /p/ vs /b/ differs, and the words mean different things. So /p/ and /b/ are separate phonemes in English.

If you can't find a minimal pair, the sounds might be allophones of the same phoneme. Linguists use this technique to map a language's sound system.

Minimal pairs are also a foundational tool in language teaching — they help learners hear distinctions their native language doesn't make.

concepts.title: Sound Rules — Assimilation
concepts.contentHtml:
Sounds influence their neighbors. Assimilation is when a sound changes to become more like a nearby sound — your mouth taking shortcuts.

Watch the prefix 'in-' attach to different roots:

— in-tolerant
— im-possible (n becomes m before p, both bilabial)
— il-legal (n becomes l before l)
— ir-regular (n becomes r before r)

The 'in-' adapts its place of articulation to match what follows. Speakers do this automatically — assimilation makes speech easier and faster. Languages everywhere show this same drift toward articulatory laziness.

concepts.title: Anatomy of a Syllable
concepts.contentHtml:
A syllable has three parts:

Onset — the consonant(s) before the vowel.
Nucleus — the vowel (or syllabic consonant) itself, the 'core'.
Coda — the consonant(s) after the vowel.

'cat' = c (onset) + a (nucleus) + t (coda).
'a' = (no onset) + a (nucleus) + (no coda).

Languages differ in what syllables they allow. English permits clusters like 'strengths' (CCCVCCC). Japanese mostly allows only CV (single consonant + vowel) — which is why 'McDonald' becomes 'Ma-ku-do-na-ru-do' in Japanese.

concepts.title: Word Stress
concepts.contentHtml:
Stress is the relative emphasis on syllables. English stress is unpredictable from spelling — you have to learn it.

PHO-to-graph
pho-TO-gra-phy
pho-to-GRA-phic

Same root, three different stress patterns. Stress changes vowel quality too: unstressed vowels often reduce to schwa (the 'uh' sound).

Languages handle stress differently. French always stresses the final syllable. Polish the second-to-last. Czech the first. English — chaos. Japanese has pitch accent rather than stress.

concepts.title: Stress Changes Meaning
concepts.contentHtml:
In English, stress can distinguish nouns from verbs spelled identically:

RE-cord (noun) vs re-CORD (verb)
PRE-sent (noun/adj) vs pre-SENT (verb)
CON-tract (noun) vs con-TRACT (verb)

The pattern: nouns stress the first syllable, verbs the second. About 100 English word pairs follow this rule.

This is essentially a tonal distinction — same phonemes, different prosody, different meaning. The line between phonetics and grammar gets blurry here.

concepts.title: Tonal Languages
concepts.contentHtml:
In tonal languages, the pitch of a syllable changes the word's meaning — not just emphasis but its very identity.

Mandarin Chinese has four tones (plus a neutral). The syllable 'ma' means:

— mā (high level) — mother
— má (rising) — hemp
— mǎ (falling-rising) — horse
— mà (falling) — to scold

Most of the world's languages are tonal — including most of East/Southeast Asia and much of Africa. English speakers often find tones initially difficult because we don't perceive pitch as identity-shaping.

concepts.title: Intonation in Non-Tonal Languages
concepts.contentHtml:
English isn't tonal, but pitch still carries meaning at the sentence level — that's intonation.

'You're going.' (statement, falling pitch)
'You're going?' (question, rising pitch)

Same words, same stress — but pitch contour signals whether you're informing or asking.

Intonation also conveys emotion, sarcasm, and emphasis. 'Oh, GREAT' (rising-falling, drawn out) means the opposite of 'Oh, great!' (high, sharp). Speech recognition still struggles with this — sarcasm is genuinely hard.

concepts.title: Pitch Accent — A Middle Ground
concepts.contentHtml:
Some languages, like Japanese and Swedish, have pitch accent — a system halfway between stress and tone.

In Japanese, the word 'hashi' can mean:

— háshi (high-low) — chopsticks
— hashí (low-high) — bridge
— hashi (flat) — edge

Like tone, pitch matters. Unlike full tonal systems, pitch accent typically uses just one or two contrasts per word, often only on a single 'accented' syllable.

Pitch accent illustrates that languages don't fall neatly into 'tonal' vs 'non-tonal' boxes — it's a spectrum.

title: Sound Change Over Time
description: Why languages drift apart — and the rules they follow

concepts.title: Sounds Drift
concepts.contentHtml:
Languages change. Sound change is the systematic alteration of pronunciation over generations.

Latin pater → French père, Spanish padre, Italian padre, English (via Old English/Germanic) father.

Tiny shifts compound. Each generation pronounces things almost like the last, but the small differences accumulate. After 1,000 years, no one understands anyone from the past.

Sound changes are usually regular — they apply to all words containing the changing sound, not just one. This regularity lets linguists reconstruct ancestral languages from descendant evidence.

concepts.title: Grimm's Law
concepts.contentHtml:
In the early 1800s, Jacob Grimm (yes, of fairy-tale fame) discovered a systematic shift between Proto-Indo-European (PIE) and the Germanic languages.

PIE *p → Germanic f (Latin pater → English father)
PIE *t → Germanic þ/th (Latin tres → English three)
PIE *k → Germanic h (Latin cor/heart → English heart)

Grimm's Law wasn't just a pattern — it was a law: regular, exceptionless (with later refinements), predictable. This was a scientific breakthrough showing language change is not random.

concepts.title: The Great Vowel Shift
concepts.contentHtml:
Between roughly 1400 and 1700, English vowels underwent a dramatic systematic change called the Great Vowel Shift.

Long vowels rose in the mouth: 'name' (formerly 'nah-meh') became 'naym'. The highest vowels diphthongized: 'time' (formerly 'teem') became 'tahym'.

This is why English spelling is so weird — spelling froze around Chaucer's pronunciation, while the sounds kept shifting underneath. 'Knight' once was pronounced 'k-nicht'. The K and GH still sit in the spelling like fossils.

Sound change is constant. Today's English speakers are mid-shift on several sounds — future English will sound different from ours.
